# Known anomalies

<!-- GENERATED by com.rapidfx.compiler.docs.KnownAnomalies.
     Do not edit. Run `./gradlew :compiler:knownAnomalies` to regenerate. -->

Everything this toolchain is known to get wrong, with what to do instead.

Two halves. The **compiler limitations** are derived by compiling a program that
provokes each one, so an entry here is evidence that the limitation is still present
and that the wording is the one you will meet. The **platform anomalies** are facts
about the runtime's C libraries and data, found by measuring against a real JDK; each
names the experiment that holds it.

> **Risk is not assessed here, and that is deliberate.** Under ISO 14971 a risk
> belongs to a hazard in a particular device, not to a defect in a tool — the same
> wrong date is an inconvenience in a stock list and something else in a dosing
> interval. These entries state what happens so that the manufacturer can classify
> it. Filling the column in from here would be making somebody else's assessment for
> them.

## Compiler limitations

The source is right and this version cannot compile it. Each reports `RFX0900` with a file and a line.

### RFXA-001 · Multi-dimensional arrays

| | |
|---|---|
| **The compiler says** | Multi-dimensional arrays cannot be compiled in this version yet (planned for later). |
| **Instead** | Use an array of arrays — Dim rows(2) As Integer(), read and written as rows(0)(0) — or a one-dimensional array with computed indices. Such an array also goes straight into a Java method that takes Integer[][]. Java collections are unaffected: an ArrayList of ArrayLists and List(Of List(Of String)) both work. |

### RFXA-002 · Compound assignment to a property

| | |
|---|---|
| **The compiler says** | Compound assignment to a property cannot be compiled in this version yet (planned for M3). |
| **Instead** | Write it out: worker.Priority = worker.Priority + 1. |

### RFXA-003 · Indexed properties

| | |
|---|---|
| **The compiler says** | Indexed properties cannot be compiled in this version yet (planned for later). |
| **Instead** | Use a method — GetItem(index) — or expose a List. |

### RFXA-004 · 'Resume'

| | |
|---|---|
| **The compiler says** | 'Resume' cannot be compiled in this version yet (planned for later — use 'Try/Catch'). |
| **Instead** | Use Try/Catch, which can express what Resume was for. |

### Branches no program can reach

The compiler carries a refusal for these, and nothing can provoke it. Listed so that the set of refusals in the compiler and the set of entries above can be held against each other — not as limitations, because a limitation nobody can meet is not one.

* **'New' for an array — write 'Dim values(9) As Integer'** — Measured on 05.10.2026: no surface syntax reaches it. The comment at the call site says "this only happens for something like New Integer(,)", and that is not so — `New Integer()`, `New Integer(9)` and `New Integer(,)` all resolve Integer as a plain type and report RFX0603, because the parser reads the parentheses as an argument list and never as an array. RapidFX has no array syntax without parentheses, so `resolveType` cannot answer with an array type here at all. Left in the compiler and out of this document until somebody decides whether the branch should go.

## Platform anomalies

### RFXA-101 · Dates after 2037 can be an hour out in a zone with daylight saving

| | |
|---|---|
| **Affects** | iOS, tsbTheMachine 27.4.0 to 27.7.0 |
| **What happens** | The time-zone rules are read from the Olson files, and the trailing POSIX rule — which is what extends a zone's rules indefinitely into the future — was not carried over. A date past 2037 in a zone that observes daylight saving could therefore be offset by an hour. |
| **Instead** | Dates up to 2037 are unaffected. Where a later date matters on a build older than 27.8.0, compute the offset from a known rule rather than from the zone. |
| **Status** | fixed in tsbTheMachine 27.8.0, and this plugin pins 27.9.0. Held against JDK 25 for every zone on the host — 194 zones get a trailing rule and 192 agree exactly — and against each zone file's own transitions, which needs no outside authority. The entry stays until a run on a device confirms it; mobile/experiments/s7-zeitzonen carries eight cases past 2037 for that run |
| **Risk** | to be assessed by the manufacturer — see above |

### RFXA-102 · A long date joins differently from JDK 25, in 14 of the 27 shipped languages

| | |
|---|---|
| **Affects** | iOS and Android, every version of tsbTheMachine from 27.5.0 |
| **What happens** | The bundled ICU is 68.2, from 2020, and CLDR has since changed how a date and a time are joined. German is the measured case: ICU 68.2 joins the full and long forms with "{1} 'um' {0}", so DateFormat produces '15. März 2026 um 12:00' where JDK 25 produces '15. März 2026, 12:00' — CLDR replaced the glue with the comma and moved the 'um' into a separate resource that ICU 68 does not know. Measured on 06.10.2026 against ICU 78.3's own source resources: 14 of the 27 shipped languages that state these patterns differ. Dutch, Spanish and Slovenian gain a comma; Danish, Finnish and Croatian lose a word; Polish, Irish and Slovenian have a different short date; and English's separator before AM/PM became U+202F, which cannot be seen on a screen. |
| **Instead** | Give an explicit pattern where the exact text matters, or format the date and the time separately. A date or a time on its own is unaffected in every language but the four with a changed short date. |
| **Status** | open — a newer ICU is the fix and is its own piece of work. The entry said until 06.10.2026 that the comma was missing and had arrived in CLDR after 68.2; both halves were wrong, and the value quoted had been written down from memory rather than measured |
| **Risk** | to be assessed by the manufacturer — see above |

### RFXA-103 · getLanguage() answers the pre-1989 ISO 639 code

| | |
|---|---|
| **Affects** | iOS and Android, tsbTheMachine up to and including 27.7.0 |
| **What happens** | Hebrew, Yiddish and Indonesian changed ISO code in 1989. The runtime stored the old one, so Locale("he").getLanguage() answered 'iw' where JDK 25 answers 'he'; likewise 'ji' for Yiddish and 'in' for Indonesian. |
| **Instead** | toLanguageTag() answers the modern code on every version, because BCP 47 requires it — a program that talks to a server in language tags never saw a difference. Only a reader of getLanguage() did. On a build older than 27.8.0, compare against Locale.of("he").getLanguage() rather than against the literal. |
| **Status** | fixed in tsbTheMachine 27.8.0, and this plugin pins 27.9.0, the way OpenJDK has done it since 17: both codes are accepted and the current one is stored, with -Djava.locale.useOldISOCodes=true to restore the old behaviour. The entry stays until a run on a device confirms it; the eighth line of mobile/experiments/s8-sprachen asks both directions |
| **Risk** | to be assessed by the manufacturer — see above |

### RFXA-105 · On iOS, the step from an answered permission dialogue to the first position is unverified

| | |
|---|---|
| **Affects** | iOS only; location |
| **What happens** | The dialogue appears with the right text, and with the permission already granted the position arrives. What has not been exercised is answering the dialogue and then receiving a position, because simctl has no programmable tap. On Android the whole sequence is verified. |
| **Instead** | Verify by hand on a device as part of acceptance. |
| **Status** | unverified — not known to be broken |
| **Risk** | to be assessed by the manufacturer — see above |
